08 · Environmental impact of our experiments (Table 4)

Every experiment logged its wall-clock time (runtime_log.json; entries re-run in marimo override the Jupyter ones). We convert time to energy with the Green Algorithms model (Lannelongue et al., 2021), ||(E = t\,(n_\text{cores}P_\text{core} + m\,P_\text{mem})\,\text{PUE}||), and energy to emissions with the carbon intensity of the electricity grid. Assumptions (stated, not measured). The defaults are those of the report: 2 cores at ||(P_\text{core}=12||) W, ||(m=4||) GB of memory at 0.3725 W/GB, PUE = 1 (a laptop; a data centre adds 10–60%), and 128.8 gCO||(_2||)/kWh (Great Britain average 2025), with 175.9 gCO||(_2||)e/kWh as an upper sensitivity value. Move the sliders to see how sensitive the totals are.

data.text/html:
Table 4: time, energy and emissions by notebook (grid: 128.8 gCO₂/kWh)

All experiments: 4.27 h, 108.8 Wh, 14.0 g CO₂e — about the energy of boiling a kettle once or twice.

Cost of a single fit at n = 40 (notebook 03)

Model choice matters more than the totals: the mock paper's degree-10 kernel model costs about as much as our sparse polynomial model per fit but is over 40 points less accurate.

Adaptation of KryptoNet-40 (notebook 05; 3 learning rates per fit, 2,560 training examples)

Adaptation reuses the energy already spent on pretraining; rank-1 LoRA trains in seconds and stores 552 numbers per task.
